title: The AI Teacher Test: Measuring the Pedagogical Ability of Blender and GPT-3 in Educational Dialogues
extended_summary:
This paper asks how to evaluate whether generative conversational models are capable of functioning as AI teachers in educational dialogues. The authors argue that existing automatic text-generation metrics are not sufficient because they do not assess pedagogical qualities such as sounding like a teacher, understanding the student, and helping the student improve. They therefore propose an AI Teacher Test based on comparative judgments between human teachers and AI-generated responses.

To build the test, the authors ran Blender and GPT-3 in parallel with human teachers on real student-teacher dialogue data from language-learning and mathematics settings. They generated candidate responses to student utterances, then had human raters compare pairs of replies in context across three pedagogical dimensions: likely said by a teacher, understanding the student, and helping the student. A Bayesian Bradley-Terry model was used to estimate latent ability scores and rank responses.

The evaluation used two dialogue corpora, but the direct human rating study focused on the Teacher-Student Chatroom Corpus in second-language learning, with crowdworkers from the UK and US serving as evaluators rather than the actual students or teachers in the dataset. The main finding is that Blender and GPT-3 can show reasonable conversational uptake, but both remain substantially behind human teachers on pedagogical ability, especially helpfulness. Blender performs better than GPT-3 overall, yet neither model matches human performance. The authors conclude that their method is a first step toward more meaningful evaluation of AI teachers and could eventually support autonomous model development.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI generative language model / chatbot family used for open-domain dialogue and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-3 (Ada and Davinci completions) to generate AI teacher responses to student utterances in educational dialogues for comparison against human teacher replies.

findings.finding_summary: In comparative judgments of teacher responses in educational dialogues, GPT-3 was rated significantly worse than human teachers on all measured pedagogical abilities. Relative to the actual teacher, mean ability differences were = -0.67 for speaking like a teacher, = -0.67 for understanding the student, and = -0.93 for helping the student (all p < .001).
findings.measure: Pairwise comparative judgments on three pedagogical dimensions: likely said by a teacher, understanding the student, helping the student

findings.finding_summary: GPT-3's responses were positively evaluated in only 33-35% of dialogue contexts across the three abilities, and 2-12% of estimates had credible intervals excluding zero. The paper reports that some GPT-3 responses were still preferred over human teacher responses in specific cases, but overall performance was substantially lower than human teachers.
findings.measure: Per-item posterior ability estimates and proportion of responses with positive alpha

quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary comparative study using human judgments and Bayesian modeling, but it is not an RCT/QED of teacher outcomes. The evidence is observational and evaluative, so it fits a lower-confidence tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported negative differences for GPT-3 vs. human teachers are large in magnitude, especially for helping the student ( = -0.93). That indicates substantial underperformance on pedagogical ability, even though the direction is adverse.
